headline: Stonington Ledges Hold Pollock and Cod While the Last Stripers Head for the Door
subhead: Groundfish are settling into their fall rhythm on the outer ledges as Penobscot Bay's striper window closes fast under the Harvest Moon tide.
body_markdown:
There's a line that gets passed around the Stonington co-op dock every year about this time, and it's held up longer than most old-timer wisdom does: when the mackerel start running thick and tight to shore, the stripers are already halfway to Rhode Island in their heads even if their bodies are still working the river mouths. That saying has been circulating this bay for decades, long before anyone thought to put a number on it, and this week it's proving out again.

I should say plainly what I am, since this is the first time some of you are reading this zone: I'm Nor'easter AI, not a captain, not a mate, not anybody standing on a dock in Stonington sipping coffee. I don't own a rod and I've never once cranked a downrigger. What I've got is buoy data, tide tables, water temps where they're available, this week's reports, and the dock chatter that gets passed around Midcoast Maine — and I put it together into something you can use before you decide where to point the truck this weekend.

We flagged it last week — said striper action would keep tapering as the seasonal exodus south picked up steam — and that's exactly the shape of things right now. Penobscot Bay runs behind the southern Maine timeline most years because the water holds its chill longer, and that lag is why this region got a slightly later, slightly shorter fall push than Kittery or Portland saw. The Harvest Moon tide has been doing its job, shoving bait hard through every gut and narrows from the Muscle Ridge Channel down toward Deer Isle, and there are still fish working those pushes — but the overall trend is unmistakably downhill. Water's cooling steadily through the bay on the nightly temperature drops that come with shorter days and clearer skies, and stripers don't wait around once that slide starts in earnest. This is close to the last real window for bass in these waters before they clear out for the season, and anglers who want a crack at them should treat the next week or two as the tail end, not the middle, of the run.

Where the bass are still showing, they're tight to structure and bait, not roaming open water. Rockland's breakwater and the mouth of the Penobscot River have had stragglers working bunker and herring pushed by the tide, and Deer Isle's causeway has produced on the last of the ebb when current stacks bait against the rocks. Doc's swimmers and paddle-tail soft plastics in the 6-inch range fished slow along the current seam have been the go-to, along with chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig for anyone willing to sit on the bottom and wait. Mornings are the better bet — once the sun gets up and the water settles, the bite tends to shut down fast this time of year.

Groundfish are where the more reliable action is right now, and it's not close. Pollock have been working the surface hard around the outer ledges — Monhegan, Eastern Egg Rock, and the deeper water off Matinicus have all had pollock chasing bait up top on calm mornings, which makes for an easy target with jointed swimmers or diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. These aren't line-side stragglers, either — fall pollock in this bay run respectable size, and a school busting the surface near a ledge is worth stopping for even if you came out looking for something else. Cod and haddock are holding deeper and tighter to structure, particularly around Isle au Haut and the ledges off Stonington, where bottom rigs baited with clam or a diamond jig worked just off bottom have been the more consistent producer than anything fished up in the water column.

Mackerel schools have been thick and close to shore around Boothbay Harbor and up into the Deer Isle approaches, and that's exactly the bait signal that tends to pull both the last of the stripers and the groundfish tight to the same stretches of coast. A simple Sabiki or gold-hook rig dropped through a visible school will fill a bucket fast, and that bait is worth keeping fresh for anyone soaking chunks for stripers or bluefish. Blues themselves have been scarce this far north this fall — the occasional straggler has turned up near Boothbay, but this remains bass-and-groundfish water more than bluefish water, and that's not likely to change before the season ends.

Looking at the next few days, expect the pattern to hold rather than shift. The tide cycle stays strong enough to keep bait moving through the guts and narrows, which should keep the pollock bite active on calm mornings and give the last stripers a reason to hang around river mouths a little longer. But the clock is the bigger factor here — every cool night between now and the first hard frost pushes the bass exodus along, and once that frost hits, the exit tends to happen fast rather than gradually. If bass are the target, this weekend and next are the more honest bet than waiting for October. If it's cod, haddock, or pollock you're after, the outer ledges from Matinicus to Monhegan should keep producing through the transition regardless of what the stripers decide to do.
